questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: Which is true concerning the blue and magenta colors used to depict airports on Sectional Aeronautical Charts?

choices.text: Airports with control towers underlying Class A, B, and C airspace are shown in blue; Class D and E airspace are magenta.
Airports with control towers underlying Class C, D, and E airspace are shown in magenta.
Airports with control towers underlying Class B, C, D, and E airspace are shown in blue.

questions.explanation:
On sectional charts, airports with control towers underlying Class B, C, D, E, or G airspace are shown in blue. Airports with no control towers are shown in magenta.

Answer (A) is incorrect. There are no airports in Class A airspace. Airports with control towers are shown in blue, all others in magenta.

Answer (B) is incorrect. Airports with control towers are shown in blue, not magenta.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: True course measurements on a Sectional Aeronautical Chart should be made at a meridian near the midpoint of the course because the

choices.text: values of isogonic lines change from point to point.
angles formed by isogonic lines and lines of latitude vary from point to point.
angles formed by lines of longitude and the course line vary from point to point.

questions.explanation:
Because meridians (lines of longitude) converge toward the poles, the angles formed by meridians and the course line may vary from point to point. Thus, course measurement should be taken at a meridian near the midpoint to of the course rather than at the departure point.

Answer (A) is incorrect. Isogonic lines are used to calculate magnetic (not true) course.

Answer (B) is incorrect. Isogonic lines are used to calculate magnetic (not true) course.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: When a dashed blue circle surrounds an airport on a sectional aeronautical chart, it will depict the boundary of

choices.text: Special VFR airspace.
Class B airspace.
Class D airspace.

questions.explanation:
On a sectional aeronautical chart, the boundary of Class D airspace is depicted by a dashed (segmented) blue circle around an airport.

Answer (A) is incorrect. There is no airspace designated as special VFR.

Answer (B) is incorrect. On a sectional chart, a solid, not dashed, blue circle that surrounds an airport depicts the boundary of Class B airspace.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: Alert Areas are special use airspace depicted within magenta lines on sectional charts in which

choices.text: there is a high volume of pilot training activities or an unusual type of aerial activity, neither of which is hazardous to aircraft.
the flight of aircraft is prohibited.
the flight of aircraft, while not prohibited, is subject to restriction.

questions.explanation:
Alert areas are depicted on charts to inform non-participating pilots of areas that may contain a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity, neither of which is hazardous to aircraft.

Answer (B) is incorrect. A prohibited area, not an alert area, is airspace within which the flight of aircraft is prohibited.

Answer (C) is incorrect. A restricted area, not an alert area, is airspace within which the flight of aircraft, while not prohibited, is subject to restriction.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: Which statement is true about isogonic lines?

choices.text: Isogonic lines are lines of equal variation.
Isogonic lines do not vary for different headings of the same aircraft.
Varies over time as the Agonic line shifts.

questions.explanation:
Isogonic lines are shown on most aeronautical charts as broken magenta lines, which connect points of equal magnetic variation. The 0° line is known as the agonic line. The agonic is the line connecting points at which there is no variation between true north and magnetic north.

Answer (B) is incorrect. If an aircraft is heading east, the isogonic lines increase in increments of 5°, e.g., +5°, +10°, +15°, etc., except the last line in the most eastern part of the United States, which is +24. If the aircraft is flying west, the isogonic lines decrease in increments of 5°, into negative numbers to the west of the agonic line, e.g., -5°, -10°, -15° etc., except the last line in the most western part of the United States, which is -24.

Answer (C) is incorrect. Over time, the isogonic and agonic lines shift due to the movement of the magnetic north pole. However, the degree of change may vary due to unusual geological conditions affecting magnetic forces in localized areas.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: Before passing through a military operation area (MOA), a pilot should

choices.text: exercise extreme caution.
avoid the MOA if flying at night.
verify the operating hours on the back of a sectional chart and contact the operating agency prior to entering the MOA.

questions.explanation:
The pilot should verify the active hours and controlling agency of the MOA. Prior to entering the MOA, the pilot must contact the controlling agency.

Answer (A) is incorrect. A pilot should exercise extreme caution during flight into an MOA. However, you must contact the controlling agency prior to entering the MOA.

Answer (B) is incorrect. The MOA should be avoided during active operations, not at night.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: When looking at a sectional chart, you see the term " R-4009. " What does this designate?

choices.text: Warning area.
Prohibited area.
Restricted area.

questions.explanation:
An " R " followed by a number designates a restricted area on a sectional chart.

Answer (A) is incorrect. A warning area is shown as " W " followed by a number.

Answer (B) is incorrect. A prohibited area is designated by a " P " followed by a number.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: How do you find out the airspace classification for a Class D airport with a part-time control tower when the tower closes for the night?

choices.text: Check the Chart Supplement.
Consult the sectional chart frequency tab.
Call the local ATIS.

questions.explanation:
The Chart Supplement page for the airport, under the Airspace section, notes the control tower hours of operation and the airspace classification. The airspace for these airports is normally Class D during tower operation and Class E or G at all other times.

Answer (B) is incorrect. The hours of operation are noted on the frequency tab, but not the airspace classification.

Answer (C) is incorrect. ATIS may inform you that the tower is closed until a specific time, but it will not inform you of the airspace classification.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 68 on page 375.) Where is Air Park Dallas located with relation to the city?

choices.text: North, approximately 9 miles.
Northeast, approximately 16 miles.
North, approximately 33 miles.

questions.explanation:
Fig. 68 contains the Chart Supplement excerpt for Air Park Dallas. On the first line, the third item listed, 16 NE, means that Air Park Dallas is located approximately 16 NM northeast of the associated city.

Answer (A) is incorrect. North, approximately 9 mi., is the approximate distance from ADS Airport to the associated city, not Air Park Dallas.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The airport is approximately 16 NM northeast, not 33 NM north, of the associated city.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 68 on page 375.) Refer to Air Park Dallas (N33°01.41' W96°50.22'). Is fuel ever available at Air Park Dallas?

choices.text: Yes, whenever the airport is attended by airport personnel.
No, since there is no " star " symbol near the airport on the chart, there is no fuel available at this airport.
Yes, fuel services can be arranged by calling the listed phone number prior to arrival.

questions.explanation:
Look at Fig. 68, the Chart Supplement excerpt for Air Park Dallas, located at the given coordinates. Locate the " Airport Remarks. " You will see on the first line that fuel is available by calling the listed phone number prior to arrival (arr).

Answer (A) is incorrect. The airport is unattended, and there are no regular fuel services available.

Answer (B) is incorrect. The star symbol on a Chart Supplement diagram represents the airport beacon, not fuel services.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: You are preflight planning in the morning before an afternoon flight. Where would you find information regarding an " Airport surface hot spot? "

choices.text: Call the Automated Flight Service Station.
In the Chart Supplements U.S.
In the NOTAMs during your preflight briefing.

questions.explanation:
An " airport surface hot spot " is a runway safety related problem area or intersection on an airport. Information regarding airport surface hot spots can be found in the Chart Supplements U.S.

Answer (A) is incorrect. Information regarding airport surface hot spots can be found in the Chart Supplements U.S.

Answer (C) is incorrect. Information regarding airport surface hot spots can be found in the Chart Supplements U.S.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 66 on page 377.) Traffic patterns in effect at Wiley Post are

choices.text: to the right on Runways 35R, 35L, and 31; to the left on Runways 1 7L, 17R, and 13.
to the left on Runways 35R, 35L, and 31; to the right on Runways 17L, 17R, and 13.
to the right on Runways 17L-35R.

questions.explanation:
Fig. 66 contains the Chart Supplement excerpt for Wiley Post. For this question, you need to locate the runway end data elements, i.e., Rwy 17L-35R, Rwy 17R-35L, to and Rwy 13-31. Traffic patterns are to the left unless right traffic is noted by the contraction " Rgt tfc. " The only runways with right traffic are Rwy 17L, 17R, and 13.

Answer (A) is incorrect. Traffic patterns are to the left, not right, for Rwy 35R, 35L, and 31. Traffic patterns are to the right, not left, for Rwy 17L, 17R, and 13.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The traffic pattern for Rwy 35R is to the left, not right.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 66 on page 377.) What is the recommended communications procedure for landing at Wiley Post during the hours when the tower is not in operation?

choices.text: Monitor airport traffic and announce your position and intentions on 126.9 MHz.
Contact UNICOM on 122.95 MHz for traffic advisories.
Monitor ATIS for airport conditions; then announce your position on 122.95 MHz.

questions.explanation:
When the Wiley Post tower is closed, you should monitor airport traffic and announce your position and intentions on the CTAF. Fig. 66 contains the Chart Supplement excerpt for Wiley Post. Locate the section titled " Communications " and note that on that same line the CTAF frequency is 126.9.

Answer (B) is incorrect. When the tower is not in operation, you should monitor other traffic and announce your position and intentions on the specified CTAF. At Wiley Post, the CTAF is the tower frequency of 126.9, not the UNICOM frequency of 122.95.

Answer (C) is incorrect. When the tower is not in operation, you should monitor other traffic and announce your position and intentions on the specified CTAF. At Wiley Post, the CTAF is the tower frequency of 126.9, not the UNICOM frequency of 122.95.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: To avoid landing at the wrong airport or runway, pilots should

choices.text: consult the Aeronautical Information Manual.
consult airport diagrams and Chart Supplements.
contact the airport UNICOM frequency for runway advisory.

questions.explanation:
Chart Supplements are published every 56 days and include the most accurate information about an airport, including runways and lighting.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The Aeronautical Information Manual does not include airport-specific information regarding runways and is used as a recommendation.

Answer (C) is incorrect. Although recommended runway information can be received on the UNICOM frequency, not all airports have active UNICOMs and it is better practice to use the Chart Supplements, which include more detailed information such as LAHSO operations.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 67 on page 379.) When approaching Lubbock Preston Smith Airport from the west at noon for the purpose of landing, initial communications should be with

choices.text: Lubbock Approach Control on 119.2 MHz.
Fort Worth Center on 128.75 MHz.
Lubbock Tower on 120.5 MHz.

questions.explanation:
Fig. 67 contains the Chart Supplement excerpt for Lubbock Preston Smith Airport. Locate the section titled " Airspace " and note that Lubbock Preston Smith Airport is located in Class C airspace. You should contact approach control (app con) before entering. Move up two lines to " APP/ DEP CON " and note that aircraft should initially contact Lubbock Approach Control on 119.2 MHz.

Answer (B) is incorrect. The frequencies shown in the communications section for App/Dep Con do not include Lubbock Preston Smith Airport, your initial contact should be with approach control, not the tower.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 67 on page 379.) Which type of radar service is provided to VFR aircraft at Lubbock Preston Smith Airport?

choices.text: Sequencing to the primary Class C airport and standard separation.
Sequencing to the primary Class C airport and limited vectoring so that radar targets do not touch, or 1,000 ft. vertical separation.
Sequencing to the primary Class C airport, traffic advisories, limited vectoring, and safety alerts.

questions.explanation:
Fig. 67 contains the Chart Supplement excerpt for Lubbock Preston Smith Airport. Locate the section titled " Airspace " to determine that Lubbock Preston Smith Airport is located in Class C airspace. Once communications and radar contact are established, VFR aircraft are provided the following services:

1. Sequencing to the primary airport do

2. Approved separation between IFR and VFR aircraft

3. Basic radar services, i.e., safety alerts, limited vectoring, and traffic advisories

Answer (A) is incorrect. In addition to sequencing to the primary Class C airport and standard separation, Class C radar service also includes basic radar services, i.e., traffic advisories and safety alerts.

Answer (B) is incorrect. One radar service provided to VFR aircraft in Class C airspace provides for traffic advisories and limited vectoring so that radar targets do not touch, or 500 ft., not 1,000 ft., of vertical separation.

AUNICOM.
UNICOM.

A solid magenta circle around an airport.
A magenta vignette that goes around an airport.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55 on page 383.) En route on V112 from BTG VORTAC to CARBY intersection, the minimum altitude crossing GYMME intersection is

choices.text: 6,400 feet.
6,500 feet.
7,000 feet.

questions.explanation:
When no minimum crossing altitude (MCA) is specified, e.g., at GYMME intersection, the intersection may be crossed at or above the preceding MEA. Since the MEA along V112 eastbound is 7,000 ft., GYMME may be crossed no lower than 7,000 ft.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This is the MOCA, not the MEA, along V112.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55 on page 383.) When en route on V448 from YKM VORTAC to BTG VORTAC, what minimum navigation equipment is required to identify LEARN intersection?

choices.text: One VOR receiver.
One VOR receiver and DME.
Two VOR receivers.

questions.explanation:
To identify LEARN INT., only one VOR receiver is required. It is important to establish yourself on V448 and maintain heading while you orient yourself to LTJ VORTAC R-285. Your position checks and tuning will need to be done quickly and accurately.

Answer (B) is incorrect. Since LEARN INT. can be determined by cross radials, only one VOR receiver is required; a DME is not.

Answer (C) is incorrect. Only one VOR receiver, not two, is required to identify LEARN INT.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55 on page 383.) En route on V468 from BTG VORTAC to ADOJA, the minimum altitude at TROTS intersection is

choices.text: 7,200 feet.

questions.explanation:
TROTS intersection (45 NM northeast of BTG VORTAC on V468 in Fig. 55) shows a minimum crossing altitude (MCA) of 11,500 ft. when northeastbound on V468.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This is the MOCA along V468, not the MCA at TROTS.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This is the MEA before TROTS, not the MCA at TROTS. Route Low Altitude Segment.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55A on page 385.) While passing near the KLICKITAT VOR, southbound on V497, contact is lost with Seattle Center. You should attempt to reestablish contact with Seattle Center on
questions.explanation:
To the southeast of the KLICKITAT VOR is a box with serrated edges. This box shows the frequency for on Seattle Center in the KLICKITAT VOR area as 119.65.

Answer (B) is incorrect. A frequency of 112.3 is the frequency for the KLICKITAT VOR, not Seattle Center. Additionally, 112.3 is underlined, indicating that the VOR has no voice capability (i.e., that there would be nothing to receive on 112.3).

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is the frequency you would use to contact Seattle Flight Service when in the vicinity of the KLICKITAT VOR, not Seattle Center.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55A on page 385.) En route on V448 from FEBUS to ANGOO, the minimum altitude crossing YKM is

choices.text: 5,000 feet.
8,500 feet.
9,500 feet.

questions.explanation:
The YKM VORTAC has a flag with an x. If you look below the Yakima VORTAC box, you will see text indicating that the MCA for V448 is 9,500 feet in the southwest direction.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The directional MEA is 5,000 feet when traveling northeast bound between HITCH intersection and YKM VORTAC, not the MCA when traveling from FEBUS to ANGOO on V448.

Answer (B) is incorrect. As you travel on V468 from east to west from YKM, the MEA is 8,500 feet.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55A on page 385.) What is the MOCA between HITCH and TROTS intersections on V468?

choices.text: 6,800 feet MSL.
7,000 feet MSL.
8,500 feet MSL.

questions.explanation:
on DISCUSSION: The MOCA (minimum obstruction clearance altitude) appears with an asterisk under the MEA on V468. It is 6,800 ft. MSL.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This is the MEA if you have GPS or WAAS equipment and you filed your IFR plan as such.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is the MEA, not MOCA, between HITCH and SWANY intersections.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 55A on page 385.) At what point should a VOR changeover be made from FEBUS intersection to YKM VORTAC southbound on V448?

choices.text: 15 NM north of YKM.
31 NM north of YKM.
45 NM north of YKM.

questions.explanation:
The VOR changeover point is depicted on V448, southwest of FEBUS intersection, and depicts the mileage between the VORTAC stations. It shows the COP as being 15 NM northeast of YKM VORTAC.

Answer (B) is incorrect. The distance between FEBUS intersection and YKM is 31 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The COP is 45 NM southwest of Moses Lake VORTAC, not Yakima VORTAC.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 30 on page 387.) What minimum navigation equipment is required to complete the VOR/DME-A procedure?

choices.text: One VOR receiver.
One VOR receiver and DME.
Two VOR receivers and DME.

questions.explanation:
The minimum navigation equipment required for a VOR/DME approach is one VOR receiver and DME.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The minimum equipment required for a VOR/DME approach includes DME.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The approach requires one VOR receiver, not two.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 30 on page 387.) The minimum safe altitude (MSA) for the VOR/DME or GPS-A at 7D3 is geographically centered on what position?

choices.text: DEANI intersection.
WHITE CLOUD VOR/DME.
MAJUB intersection.

questions.explanation:
Minimum safe altitudes provide obstacle clearance within 25 NM of the specified navigational facility. In Fig. 30, the MSA circle specifies WHITE CLOUD VOR/DME.

Answer (A) is incorrect. DEANI intersection is the point of descent to the final approach fix.

Answer (C) is incorrect. An MSA will normally be based on a navigation facility or a waypoint (GPS or RNAV approach), not the airport.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 30 on page 387.) When approaching the VOR/DME-A, the symbol [2800] in the MSA circle represents a minimum safe sector altitude within 25 NM of

choices.text: DEANI intersection.
White Cloud VOR/DME.
Baldwin Municipal Airport.

questions.explanation:
in DISCUSSION: For conventional navigation systems, the MSA is normally based on the primary omnidirectional facility on which the IAP is predicated. The MSA depiction in Fig. 30 contains the facility identifier of White Cloud VOR/DME. MSAs are expressed in feet above mean sea level and normally have a 25 NM radius; however, this radius may be expanded to 30 NM if necessary to encompass the airport landing surfaces.

Answer (A) is incorrect. DEANI intersection is the point of descent to the final approach fix, not the point of reference for the MSA.

Answer (C) is incorrect. White Cloud VOR/DME is the designated point of reference for the MSA, not Baldwin Municipal Airport.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 28 on page 389.) When conducting a missed approach from the LOC RWY 31 approach at KDSM, what is the Minimum Safe Altitude (MSA) while maneuvering?

choices.text: 1,600 feet.
2,800 feet.
4,000 feet.

questions.explanation:
The approach plate indicates that 2,800 feet MSL is the MSA in the sector in which maneuvering for the missed approach occurs. Minimum safe altitudes are published for emergency use on IAP. MSAs provide 1,000 feet of clearance over all obstacles but do not necessarily assure acceptable navigation signal coverage. The MSA depiction on the plan view of an approach chart contains the identifier of the center point of the MSA, the applicable radius of the MSA, a depiction of the sector(s), and the minimum altitudes above MSL which provide obstacle clearance.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The initial altitude to climb to in the missed approach procedure is 1,600 feet.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The MSA from the DSM 330 through 060 degree radials is 4,000 feet. Additionally, 4,000 feet is the emergency safe altitude from 25 NM to 100 NM from DSM. When conducting the missed approach procedure hold, the inbound turn commences at 22 NM DME, which would keep the outermost turning radius within the 25 NM MSA protected area.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 28 on page 389.) During the ILS RWY 31 procedure at DSM, the minimum altitude for glide slope interception is

choices.text: 2,365 feet MSL.
2,400 feet MSL.
3,000 feet MSL.

questions.explanation:
for DISCUSSION: The minimum glide slope interception altitude for an ILS is the FAF (marked by a lightning bolt). In Fig. 28, the FAF is 2,400 ft. MSL.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This is the glide slope altitude over the LOM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is the MSA when south of the LOM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 27 on page 391.) Refer to the DEN ILS RWY 35R procedure. The FAF intercept altitude is

choices.text: 6,120 feet MSL.
5,570 feet MSL.
7,000 feet MSL.

questions.explanation:
The glide slope intercept altitude at the FAF (lightning bolt) is 7,000 feet MSL.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The minimum altitude for the nonprecision approach is 6,120 feet MSL.

Answer (B) is incorrect The DH is 5,570 feet MSL.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 27 on page 391.) Which reported ground visibility at DEN is the lowest that a flight crew could use for this approach?

choices.text: 1/4 mile.
1/2 mile.
RVR10.

questions.explanation:
a DISCUSSION: The conversion from 1/2 mi. visibility to RVR is 2400, and 1/4 mi. is 1600 RVR. The approach requires at least 1800 RVR. Therefore, of the choices provided, the lowest reported ground visibility acceptable for the approach is 1/2 mi.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The conversion from 1/4 mi. visibility to RVR is 1600. This approach requires a minimum of 1800 RVR. Therefore, a 1/4 mi. visibility is not an acceptable ground visibility to use this approach.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The RVR needs to be equal to or greater than 1800 (RVR 18).

questions.question: (Refer to Figure 27 on page 391.) The symbol on the plan view of the ILS RWY 35R procedure at DEN represents a minimum safe sector altitude within 25 NM of

GLLVORTAC.
Denver International Airport.

questions.explanation:
Minimum safe altitudes provide obstacle clearance within 25 NM of the specified navigational facility. In Fig. 27, the MSA circle specifies DEN VOR/DME.

Answer (B) is incorrect. An MSA for the ILS RWY 35R at DEN is based on Denver VOR/DME, not the GLL VORTAC.

Answer (C) is incorrect. An MSA will always be based on a navigation facility or a waypoint (GPS or RNAV approach), not an airport.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 26 on page 393.) The final approach fix for the precision approach is located at

choices.text: RIIVR intersection.
Glide slope intercept (lightning bolt).
JETSA intersection.

questions.explanation:
at DISCUSSION: On a precision approach, the final approach fix is the glide slope intercept point at the published altitude. It is identified on an IAP chart by a lightning bolt.

Answer (A) is incorrect. RIIVR intersection is an IAF, not the FAF.

Answer (C) is incorrect. JETSA intersection is the FAF for the LOC 24R, not the ILS 24R, approach.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 26 on page 393.) During the ILS RWY 24R procedure at LAX, what altitude minimum applies if the glide slope becomes inoperative?

choices.text: 580 feet.
460 feet.
320 feet.

questions.explanation:
If the glide slope fails during an ILS approach, the approach can be continued as a nonprecision localizer approach. The MDA for the LOC RWY 24R is 460 ft.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This is the sidestep, not straightin, MDA for Categories A, B, and C.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is the DH for the ILS, not the MDA for the localizer.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: (Refer to Figure 26 on page 393.) The final approach fix for the ILS RWY 24R is located at

choices.text: MERCE intersection.
Glide Slope Intercept (lightning bolt).
JETSA intersection.

questions.explanation:
The final approach fix for an ILS approach is indicated on an instrument approach procedure by a lightning bolt symbol. This is also the point of glide slope intercept.

Answer (A) is incorrect. The MERCE intersection is an intermediate fix (indicated by the " IF " notation), not the final approach fix.

Answer (C) is incorrect. The Maltese cross symbol indicates that JETSA is the final approach fix for the nonprecision localizer approach, not for the precision ILS approach.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an airplane is consuming 95 pounds of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 6,500 feet and the groundspeed is 173 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 450 NM?

choices.text: 248 pounds.
265 pounds.
284 pounds.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 173 kt., it will take 2.60 hr. to go 450 NM (450 NM - 173 NM/hr.). At 95 lb./hr„ it will take approximately 248 lb. (2.60 x 95) of fuel.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This is required to travel 483 NM, not 450 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is required to travel 517 NM, not 450 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If fuel consumption is 80 pounds per hour and groundspeed is 180 knots, how much fuel is required for an airplane to travel 477 NM?

choices.text: 205 pounds.
212 pounds.
460 pounds.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 180 kt., it will take 2.65 hr. to go 477 NM (477 NM - 180 NM/hr.). At 80 lb./hr„ it will take approximately 212 lb. (2.65 x 80) of fuel.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This is required to travel 461 NM, not 477 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is required to travel 1,035 NM, not 477 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If fuel consumption is 80 pounds per hour and groundspeed is 180 knots, how much fuel is required for an airplane to travel 460 NM?

choices.text: 205 pounds.
212 pounds.
460 pounds.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 180 kt., it will take 2.56 hr. to go 460 NM (460 NM - 180 NM/hr.). At 80 lb./hr„ it will take approximately 205 lb. (2.56 hr. x 80 Ib./hr.) of fuel.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This is required to travel 477 NM, not 460 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This is required to travel 1,035 NM, not 460 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an airplane is consuming 12.5 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 8,500 feet and the groundspeed is 145 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 435 NM?

choices.text: 27 gallons.
34 gallons.
38 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 145 kt., it will take 3.0 hr. to go 435 NM (435 NM - 145 NM/hr.). At 12.5 GPH, it will take approximately 38 gal. (3 x 12.5) of fuel.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 313 NM, not 435 NM.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 394 NM, not 435 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an airplane is consuming 9.5 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 6,000 feet and the groundspeed is 135 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 490 NM?

choices.text: 27 gallons.
30 gallons.
35 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 135 kt., it will take 3.63 hr. to go 490 NM (490 NM - 135 NM/hr.). At 9.5 GPH, it will take approximately 35 gal. (3.63 x 9.5) of fuel.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 384 NM, not 490 NM.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 426 NM, not 490 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an aircraft is consuming 9.7 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 6,000 feet and the groundspeed is 115 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 350 NM?

choices.text: 36 gallons.
30 gallons.
41 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 115 kt., it will take 3.04 hr. to go 350 NM (350 NM * 115 NM/hr.). At 9.7 GPH, it will take approximately 30 gal. (3.04 hr. x 9.7 GPH) of fuel.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 426 NM, not 350 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 490 NM, not 350 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an aircraft is consuming 9.3 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 6,000 feet and the groundspeed is 135 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 390 NM?

choices.text: 27 gallons.
30 gallons.
35 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 135 kt., it will take 2.89 hr. to go 390 NM (390 NM - 135 NM/hr.). At 9.3 GPH, it will take approximately 27 gal. (2.89 hr. x 9.3 GPH) of fuel.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 435 NM, not 390 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 510 NM, not 390 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an aircraft is consuming 9.5 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 6,000 feet and the groundspeed is 135 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 380 NM?

choices.text: 27 gallons.
30 gallons.
35 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 135 knots, it will take 2.81 hr. to go 380 NM (380 NM - 135 NM/hr.). At 9.5 GPH, it will take approximately 27 gal. (2.81 hr. x 9.5 GPH) of fuel.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 427 NM, not 380 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 497 NM, not 380 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an aircraft is consuming 9.5 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 6,000 feet and the groundspeed is 135 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 420 NM?

choices.text: 27 gallons.
30 gallons.
35 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 135 knots, it will take 3.11 hr. to go 420 NM (420 NM - 135 NM/hr.). At 9.5 GPH, it will take approximately 30 gal. (3.11 hr. x 9.5 gal./hr.) of fuel.

Answer (A) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 384 NM, not 420 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 497 NM, not 420 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If an airplane is consuming 14.8 gallons of fuel per hour at a cruising altitude of 7,500 feet and the groundspeed is 167 knots, how much fuel is required to travel 560 NM?

choices.text: 50 gallons.
53 gallons.
57 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 167 kt., it will take 3.35 hr. to go 560 NM (560 NM - 167 NM/hr.). At 14.8 GPH, it will take approximately 50 gal. (3.35 x 14.8) of fuel.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 598 NM, not 560 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 643 NM, not 560 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question: If fuel consumption is 14.7 gallons per hour and groundspeed is 157 knots, how much fuel is required for an airplane to travel 612 NM?

choices.text: 58 gallons.
60 gallons.
64 gallons.

questions.explanation:
At a groundspeed of 157 kt., it will take 3.90 hr. to go 612 NM (612 NM - 157 NM/hr.). At 14.7 GPH, it will take approximately 58 gal. (3.90 x 14.7) of fuel.

Answer (B) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 641 NM, not 612 NM.

Answer (C) is incorrect. This amount is required to travel 684 NM, not 612 NM.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question:
GIVEN:
True course 105°
True heading 085°
True airspeed 95 kts
Groundspeed 87 kts
Determine the wind direction and speed.

choices.text: 020° and 32 knots.
030° and 38 knots.
200° and 32 knots.

questions.explanation:
To estimate your wind, given a true heading and a true course, simply use the wind side of your flight computer backwards. First, place your groundspeed of 87 kt. under the grommet with your true course of 105° under the true index. Since your true heading is 085°, you are holding a 20° left wind correction angle. Next, place a pencil mark on the 95-kt. true airspeed arc, 20° left of the centerline. Finally, rotate the wheel until the pencil mark is on the centerline, and read a wind of 020° (under the true index) at 32 kt. (up from the grommet).

Answer (B) is incorrect. A wind from 030° at 38 kt. would result in less wind correction and a slower groundspeed.

Answer (C) is incorrect. A wind from 200° at 32 kt. would result in a higher, not lower, groundspeed than airspeed.

questions.subject: CPL Gleim
questions.question:
GIVEN:
True course 345°
True heading 355°
True airspeed 85 kts
Groundspeed 95 kts
Determine the wind direction and speed.

choices.text: 095° and 19 knots.
113° and 19 knots.
238° and 18 knots.

questions.explanation:
To estimate your wind, given a true heading and a true course, use the wind side of your flight computer backwards. First, place your groundspeed of 95 kt. under the grommet with your true course of 345° under the true index. Since your true heading is 355°, you are holding a 10° right wind correction angle. Next, place a pencil mark on the 85-kt. true airspeed arc, 10° right ofcenterline. Finally, rotate the wheel until the pencil mark is on the centerline, and read a wind of 113° (under the true index) at 19 kt. (up from the grommet).

Answer (A) is incorrect. A wind from 095° at 19 kt. would result in more wind correction angle and a slower groundspeed.

Answer (C) is incorrect. A wind from 238° at 18 kt. would require a left, not right, wind correction angle.
